faqs.question: How do you say "I love you" in Nepali?
faqs.answer: म तिमीलाई माया गर्छु (ma timīlāī māyā garchhu). The word doing the work is माया (māyā), which Turner's 1931 Nepali dictionary glosses on p. 504 as "Infatuation, folly; — (pop.) magic; — love; pity". The sentence is assembled from Turner's माया entry and his note under गर्नु (p. 137) that it is "frequently used with substantives to form verbal expressions".

faqs.question: Should I use तिमी or तपाईं when I write to my girlfriend?
faqs.answer: तिमी. Turner records तिमि as "less familiar than tã, less formal than tapāĩ" and used "between friends", which is the register a partner sits in. तपाईं to a girlfriend reads as distance or as a joke, and तँ can read as intimate or as contempt depending on who you already are to her.

faqs.question: What is the shortest love letter I can send in Nepali?
faqs.answer: Three lines is enough: प्यारी (pyārī, "dear, darling"), म तिमीलाई माया गर्छु, and माया न मार (māyā na māra, "don't forget me"). The last is printed verbatim in Turner on p. 504, so it is one of the few short Nepali love lines you can point at a source for.

faqs.question: Is a Nepali love letter the same as a Hindi one written in Devanagari?
faqs.answer: No. The script is shared but the grammar is not. Nepali uses तिमी हौ where Hindi uses तुम हो, and Turner treats छनु (chanu) as its own verb on p. 191 with the present tense "chu, chas, cha, chaũ, chau, chan" — nothing in that paradigm resembles Hindi है.

faqs.question: What does माया actually mean in Nepali?
faqs.answer: Turner lists four senses on p. 504: "Infatuation, folly; — (pop.) magic; — love; pity", from Sanskrit माया, "art". Love is a listed dictionary sense of the word in Nepali, which is why a Nepali letter reaches for माया rather than a Hindi equivalent.

faqs.question: How do I write a heart touching love letter for my girlfriend in Nepali?
faqs.answer: Pick the longing line rather than the declaration. मेरो मुटु पिलिन्छ (mero muṭu pilincha in Turner's romanisation) is his own example under मुटु on p. 512, glossed "to be full of anxiety", and it does more emotional work than a plain "I love you" because it names a physical feeling.

faqs.question: Can I send a Nepali love letter in Roman script instead of Devanagari?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should if that is what she reads. Many Nepali speakers type the language in Roman script by default, and Devanagari she has to squint at is an obstacle rather than a gift. Keep the romanisation internally consistent — this post uses chh for छ and ch for च.

faqs.question: Are there Nepali love quotes I can use instead of writing my own?
faqs.answer: There is one worth borrowing and it is a warning, not a compliment: मायाले काया हुँदैन (māyā le kāyā hũdaina), "the body does not live by love", printed as a proverb under माया on p. 504. It works as an honest line in a letter that is also about distance or money.

faqs.question: What is a good short love message for a girlfriend in Nepali over chat?
faqs.answer: मलाई माया लाग्यो (malāi māyā lāgyo), "I have fallen in love." It is Turner's own example sentence on p. 504, romanisation included, so it is the rare Nepali message you can verify before you send it rather than after.

faqs.question: Does this work if my girlfriend grew up in Darjeeling or Sikkim rather than Nepal?
faqs.answer: Yes. Nepali is one of the 22 languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, so it is an Indian language as well as Nepal's. The register advice does not change; what changes is that Roman-script Nepali is more common in some Indian Nepali-speaking communities.

faqs.question: Do I need her to be able to read Devanagari?
faqs.answer: For a Devanagari letter, yes — and that is worth checking before you write one. If you are unsure, send the romanisation alongside the script rather than instead of it, which is how this post presents every line.

faqs.question: Was the Nepali in this post checked by a native speaker?
faqs.answer: Not yet. Every line is traced to a page in Turner's 1931 dictionary, and the four assembled lines are labelled as assembled, but native review is pending and the specific lines under question are listed in this post's internal audit. Treat the four assembled lines as verified in their parts, not as attested sentences.

article.contentMarkdown:
# A Love Letter for Girlfriend in Nepali, Line by Line

A love letter for girlfriend in Nepali turns on one grammatical choice before you write a word: तिमी (timī), not तपाईं (tapāĩ). Turner's 1931 dictionary of Nepali [records तिमि as "less familiar than tã, less formal than tapāĩ"](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/turnernepali_query.py?qs=%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%BF&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact), used "between friends", and — the part almost every sample letter online gets wrong — "it takes the second person plural of the verb."

This post gives eight Nepali lines with a page number attached to each, so you can check them yourself. It is grounded in the template SubhSandesh's users reach for hardest: the "I love you" page is 987 of the 3,377 pages created on the platform since 2026-03-12, and it has drawn 14,607 views, 35.2% of every view recorded.

Those numbers count every SubhSandesh page in every language: the database stores no page-language field, so none of them is a Nepali-speaker figure.

## What is a Nepali प्रेमपत्र (prem patra)?

A प्रेमपत्र is a love letter written in Nepali, in Devanagari script, using the affectionate second person तिमी and the Nepali word माया. Turner glosses पत्र (patra) as "letter; document, deed", so प्रेमपत्र is a transparent compound: love plus letter.

What makes it a *Nepali* letter rather than a Hindi one transliterated is grammar, not vocabulary. The copula differs, the verb endings differ, and the second-person system has more rungs than Hindi's two.

A note on how the Nepali here is written. Devanagari follows modern standard spelling (तिमी, तिमीलाई); romanisations use macrons for long vowels, `~` for nasalisation, `chh` for छ and `ch` for च.

Quotations keep Turner's own 1931 spelling and romanisation verbatim — he headwords तिमि with a short i and writes `ch` for छ. The two systems disagree, so both are shown rather than silently merged.

## Which "you" do you use — तँ, तिमी or तपाईं?

Use तिमी. Turner makes the three-way contrast explicit: [तँ (tã) is "used in very familiar address, or by a superior to his greatly inferior"](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/turnernepali_query.py?qs=%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%81&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact), and तिमि sits above it, below तपाईं. To a girlfriend तपाईं reads as distance or as a joke; तँ reads as intimate or as contempt depending entirely on who you already are to her.

This is not settled etiquette but a live grammatical system, and Nepali linguists disagree on how many rungs it has. Lekhnath Sharma Pathak's 2019 paper in *Gipan* treats ["the canonical three-level honorific system" as a reference point](https://www.nepjol.info/index.php/gipan/article/view/35458) for what he calls psychologically motivated fluctuation, and reports that the significant influences on which honorific a speaker picks are "fluctuation in state of mind and proximality." Mohan Kumar Tumbahang's 2022 paper in *Dristikon* describes something wider: ["The Nepali language exhibits the five-layered honorific pronominal subjects with parallel verb conjugations"](https://www.nepjol.info/index.php/dristikon/article/view/46130).

Three levels or five, the consequence is the same: in Nepali the pronoun changes the verb. तिमी takes the second-person plural, so it is तिमी हौ, not तिमी हो. Pathak's data set includes the language of marital discord — honorific choice moves with feeling, which is why a letter is a place to decide it rather than default into it.

## Eight Nepali lines for a love letter, each one checkable

Each line gives the Devanagari, a romanisation, the meaning, and where it is verified. Four are quoted from Turner as printed. Four are assembled from words he documents separately, and are marked as assembled — that distinction matters more than a longer list would.

### 1. प्यारी

*pyārī* — "dear, loved, darling", feminine.

- **Verified**: Turner, p. 382, under पियारो (piyāro, "or pyāro"): "Affection, love, fondness… adj. (f. -i) Dear, loved, darling."
- **Use**: as the salutation; the same entry gives प्यारो गर्नु, "to love, like".

### 2. मलाई माया लाग्यो

*malāi māyā lāgyo* — "I have fallen in love."

- **Verified**: Turner, p. 504, printed as an example under माया in exactly this form.
- **Use**: the strongest line here, because nothing about it is assembled — it is a dictionary example sentence, romanisation included.

### 3. म तिमीलाई माया गर्छु

*ma timīlāī māyā garchhu* — "I love you."

- **Assembled**: माया from p. 504, गर्नु from p. 137, where Turner notes it is "frequently used with substantives to form verbal expressions."
- **Note**: the full sentence is not printed in Turner.

### 4. तिमी मेरो हौ

*timī mero hau* — "you are mine."

- **Assembled**: हौ is the तिमी form in Turner's हुनु paradigm on p. 641 (`hũ, hos, ho, haũ, hau, hun`).
- **Use**: this is where a Hindi habit does the most damage — तिमी हो is wrong.

### 5. मेरो मुटु पिलिन्छ

*mero muṭu pilincha*, in Turner's romanisation — "my heart is full of anxiety."

- **Verified**: Turner, p. 512 — मुटु (muṭu) is "The heart; feelings; courage", and `mero m˚ pilincha` is his example of मुटु पिलिनु, "to be full of anxiety."

### 6. म तिमीलाई सम्झन्छु

*ma timīlāī samjhanchhu* — "I think of you."

- **Assembled**: सम्झनु, p. 588, "To remember; understand; feel."
- **Use**: the third gloss is the useful one — this carries more warmth than "I remember you" does in English.

### 7. अँगालो मार्नु

*ãgālo mārnu* — "to embrace, to clasp."

- **Verified**: Turner, p. 1, under अँगालो: "The bent arm; armful; embrace", with `ã˚ mārnu` glossed "to embrace, to clasp".
- **Use**: kept as the phrase, because the conjugated forms are not in the entry.

### 8. माया न मार

*māyā na māra* — "don't forget me."

- **Verified**: Turner, p. 504, printed verbatim under माया मार्नु, "to forget."
- **Use**: the literal sense is "don't kill the love", and it is the best closing line in Nepali precisely because it does not translate cleanly.

Two more words worth having: सधैँ (sadhaĩ), "always", p. 583, and पर्खनु (parkhanu), "To wait, remain; — have patience", p. 367 — assembled into म सधैँ पर्खन्छु, *ma sadhaĩ parkhanchhu*, "I will always wait."

If you want the letter typed out on screen instead of pasted into a chat window, the [SubhSandesh "I love you" page](https://subhsandesh.in/love-gf) types it across its cover and keeps photos, a Love Quiz and a Truth-or-Dare round behind separate tabs. For a darker register, the [Darling romantic page](https://subhsandesh.in/darling) is the other one people pick — 349 pages, 10.3% of everything created.

## Nepali is not Hindi in Devanagari: three places they split

The script is shared; the language is not. If you have only ever written Hindi, these are where the leak happens.

**The copula.** Hindi तुम हो, Nepali तिमी हौ. Turner's हुनु paradigm on p. 641 lists `hau` for the second-person plural — the form तिमी requires.

**छ, not है.** Turner treats छनु (chanu) as a separate verb on p. 191, "To exist, be alive, be", and prints its present tense: `chu, chas, cha, chaũ, chau, chan` — so म छु, तिमी छौ. Nothing in that paradigm resembles Hindi है.

**माया as a word for love.** Turner's माया entry on p. 504 glosses it "Infatuation, folly; — (pop.) magic; — love; pity", from Sanskrit माया, "art". Love is a listed dictionary sense of माया in Nepali — which is why it is the word a Nepali letter reaches for.

One orthographic gap worth knowing: Turner's 1931 headword is तिमि, short i; modern standard Nepali writes तिमी. Neither is a typo — the spelling standardised in between.

## How the letter actually reaches her

Four routes, with the constraint each imposes. The last column is SubhSandesh's own data, counting all pages in all languages; it is not a Nepali-specific figure.

| Delivery route | What she needs | Devanagari renders | SubhSandesh signal (all pages, all languages) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Posted handwritten letter | A postal address | Your own handwriting | — |
| Pasted into a chat message | A device with a Devanagari font | Depends on her installed fonts | 50.3% of views are on a phone |
| Shared SubhSandesh page | One link | Rendered by the page itself | 987 /love-gf pages, 14,607 views |
| Shared page with a password set | The link plus the password | Same | 42.8% of creators set a password |

The takeaway is narrow: a page beats a paste for Devanagari because it controls its own typeface instead of borrowing hers.

## If she grew up in Darjeeling or Sikkim, not Nepal

Nepali is not only Nepal's language. It is one of the 22 languages [listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution](https://rajbhasha.gov.in/en/languages-included-eighth-schedule-indian-constitution), so the audience for this phrase straddles Nepal, Darjeeling, Sikkim, Assam and the diaspora.

Here honesty is cheaper than a guess. The 3,377 pages, the 987 on /love-gf and the 42.8% who set a password are platform-wide totals. The database records no language attribute on a page, so we cannot tell you how many were written in Nepali, and any post that gives you a Nepali-speaker breakdown of platform data is inventing it.

What the data does support is a workflow claim: 99.5% of started pages get published and shared, and the median gap between first save and last edit is 7.2 hours on /love-gf. Writing in a script you are not fluent in, that gap is the useful part — it is time to get the lines checked.

## When a Nepali love letter is the wrong choice

Turner records a Nepali proverb under माया on p. 504: `māyā le kāyā hũdaina`, "the body does not live by love." It is a fair corrective for a page like this one.

A letter in a script you cannot read is a risk you take with her, not for her. If your Nepali is assembled from a dictionary and she is fluent, she will see the seams — and eight lines from a source you can name land better than forty you cannot vouch for. If she reads Nepali only in Roman script, Devanagari is an obstacle rather than a gift.

A shared page is the wrong medium in two cases. If she is in the same room, hand her paper. And if the letter is really about absence rather than declaration, the [I miss you page](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) fits better.

## Sources

- R. L. Turner, *A Comparative and Etymological Dictionary of the Nepali Language* (1931), digitised by Digital Dictionaries of South Asia, University of Chicago — [माया, p. 504](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/turnernepali_query.py?qs=%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact) and [तिमि, p. 284](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/turnernepali_query.py?qs=%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%BF&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact).
- Lekhnath Sharma Pathak, ["Honorification in Nepali: a psycholinguistic perspective"](https://www.nepjol.info/index.php/gipan/article/view/35458), *Gipan*, 31 December 2019.
- Mohan Kumar Tumbahang, ["A Case of Lenition-Fortition and Honorific Asymmetry in Limbu Native's Nepali Speech"](https://www.nepjol.info/index.php/dristikon/article/view/46130), *Dristikon: A Multidisciplinary Journal* 12(1), 110–120, 5 July 2022.
- Department of Official Language, Government of India, ["Languages Included in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution"](https://rajbhasha.gov.in/en/languages-included-eighth-schedule-indian-constitution). The page states no publication date.
- First-party figures are from SubhSandesh's own database, measured 2026-09-02.

auditReport.honestAssessment:
It is the only page on this query where every Nepali line carries a page number in R. L. Turner's 1931 Comparative and Etymological Dictionary of the Nepali Language, and the only one that treats the तँ/तिमी/तपाईं choice as a grammatical decision with a source rather than a style note — four of the eight lines (मलाई माया लाग्यो p. 504, मेरो मुटु पिलिन्छ p. 512, अँगालो मार्नु p. 1, माया न मार p. 504) are printed in Turner as given. The measured SERP is Pinterest pins, 2010–2011 blogspots and one publisher's sample-letter pages with no romanisation, no register guidance and no citations, so the differentiator is real; domain authority is not, and this will take months if it moves at all. Do not predict a ranking from it.

READ FIRST — Nepali lines I am not certain of, by line. I am not a native speaker and native review is pending. Twelve flags:
(1) तिमी मेरो हौ — HIGHEST RISK. मेरो may need to agree with the feminine addressee as मेरी (तिमी मेरी हौ). Turner's हुनु paradigm (p. 641) supports हौ but says nothing about the possessive predicate's gender. Check this before publishing; it is the line most likely to be wrong.
(2) म तिमीलाई माया गर्छु — गर्छु (1sg present of गर्नु) is not printed in Turner; the -छु ending is inferred from his छनु paradigm (p. 191, "chu") and "hunchu" in the हुनु entry. Confirm the ending and the तिमीलाई dative in this frame.
(3) म तिमीलाई सम्झन्छु — सम्झन्छु not printed in Turner (only सम्झनु, p. 588). Confirm the form, and whether a letter would prefer a progressive (सम्झिरहेको छु).
(4) म सधैँ पर्खन्छु — पर्खन्छु not printed (only पर्खनु, p. 367). Confirm the form and whether पर्खनु needs an object here.
(5) प्यारी as a standalone salutation — Turner gives the feminine adjective ending -i under पियारो (p. 382) but no vocative attestation. Confirm it does not read stilted as "Dear ___".
(6) मेरो मुटु पिलिन्छ — quoted from Turner p. 512, but his romanisation is "pilincha" and the Devanagari spelling पिलिन्छ is mine. Confirm the spelling and whether मुटु पिलिनु is still current rather than 1931-archaic.
(7) माया न मार — Turner p. 504 verbatim. Confirm the negative imperative न मार is still natural, and whether a 2026 reader hears "don't forget me" or the literal "don't kill the love".
(8) अँगालो मार्नु — Turner p. 1. Confirm it is not regionally marked and that a modern reader would not prefer अँगालो हाल्नु, which Turner also lists.
(9) म छु / तिमी छौ — Devanagari spellings are mine; Turner prints only romanised "chu … chau" (p. 191). Confirm.
(10) मायाले काया हुँदैन — Turner prints "māyā le kāyā hũdaina" as three tokens; I wrote मायाले as one word. Confirm the modern conjunct spelling.
(11) The claim that तिमी हो is wrong (as against तिमी हौ) is asserted from Turner's paradigm. Confirm it is genuinely ungrammatical rather than merely non-standard.
(12) Romanisation scheme — the post declares chh for छ and ch for च, while Turner uses ch for छ and c for च, and keeps his spellings inside quotations. This was spot-checked, not exhaustively verified line by line; check that no quoted and unquoted romanisation has been silently merged.

Other honest limits. Both NepJOL papers were read as abstracts plus full bibliographic metadata on their article pages — the PDF galleys returned HTTP 500 on every attempt, so the full texts were not read, and every claim made from them is a phrase quoted from the abstract shown on the linked page. I could not reach nepjol.info/index.php/gipan/about, so Gipan's peer-review statement is unverified; the paper is described as scholarly on the basis of the journal, the DOI (10.3126) and the author's affiliation with the Central Department of Linguistics, Tribhuvan University, which the article page states. A SOAS dissertation on the Nepali public sphere in India (eprints.soas.ac.uk/34025) would have been the strongest source for the India/Nepal section, but the host was unreachable from this environment on four attempts and it is therefore not cited. On the source caps: at the time of writing, three of the batch's ten blog files existed (malayalam, nepali, never-have-i-ever), and none of this post's five URLs or three domains — dsal.uchicago.edu, www.nepjol.info, rajbhasha.gov.in — appears in any sibling, so no cap is breached. dsal.uchicago.edu and www.nepjol.info each appear twice as URLs inside this one post, which is one post against the cap, not two. The forward risk is rajbhasha.gov.in: the remaining language posts in this batch (Assamese, Punjabi, and Malayalam if it adds one) are likely to reach for the same Eighth Schedule page, which would push that domain toward the three-post limit. That is the same URL already named in the swap-test failure above and is the one to drop if the orchestrator has to choose; I have not dropped it myself. Pricing is a genuine content gap: the Pricing block in facts.md is empty, so the post makes no claim about cost in any direction, and readers arriving on an "is it free" intent are not served. That gap is recorded here rather than in the body — the draft carried a reader-facing line saying the pricing data "was not available when this was written", which is a note about the post's own production rather than an answer to the query, and it has been removed with nothing put in its place. It closes when the manual Pricing section of facts.md is filled in by hand. One structural change from the fix pass, for the record: the eight line-blocks are now a lead line plus labelled bullets instead of four-sentence paragraphs, which keeps every Devanagari form, every romanisation and every page number and closes the paragraph-length item; the swap-test and slug items are argued rather than fixed and remain in `failed`. Finally, the post's Devanagari renders only where the reader's device has a Devanagari font; nothing in the batch pipeline checks that.
